readingInstruction: Read Ezra 9:1-10:44. Ezra discovers that many in Israel have married women from the surrounding peoples, who worship other gods. He responds with grief and prayer, and the people respond with repentance. This is a hard passage. Read it carefully.
settingTheScene: Soon after Ezra arrives, the leaders report that the people, including priests and Levites, have taken wives from the peoples of the land, adopting their abominations. The concern is not ethnic. The law forbade intermarriage with the Canaanite nations because it would draw Israel into idolatry (Deuteronomy 7:1-4). The same law welcomed foreigners like Rahab and Ruth who came to worship the LORD. The issue here is covenant faithfulness.
observation: “As soon as I heard this, I tore my garment and my cloak and pulled hair from my head and beard and sat appalled” (9:3).
“O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift my face to you, my God, for our iniquities have risen higher than our heads” (9:6).
“And now, for a brief moment, grace has been shown by the LORD our God, who has left us a remnant” (9:8).
“Our God has not forsaken us in our slavery, but has extended to us his steadfast love in the sight of the kings of Persia” (9:9).
“O LORD, God of Israel, you are righteous, for we are left a remnant that has escaped, as it is this day” (9:15).
“While Ezra prayed and made confession, weeping and casting himself down before the house of God, a very great assembly of men, women, and children gathered” (10:1).
“Shecaniah… said to Ezra, We have broken faith with our God… But even now there is hope for Israel in spite of this” (10:2).
“Arise, for it is your task, and we are with you; be strong and do it” (10:4).
interpretation:
Ezra’s response is not anger at others. He tears his garment, pulls his hair, and sits appalled until the evening sacrifice. Then he prays on his knees. His prayer is a model. He says “we,” not “they.” He had not married foreign wives himself, but he identifies with the people. He is ashamed. “Our iniquities have risen higher than our heads.” He recalls the history of exile as the result of such sins. And he admits that they have done it again, after all God’s mercy.

The key note is grace. “For a brief moment, grace has been shown by the LORD our God.” Even in the middle of the confession, he acknowledges that being back in the land is itself a gift, “a little reviving in our slavery.” He does not ask for anything. He simply puts himself and the people before the righteous God: “We cannot stand before you because of this.”

The prayer moves the people. A great crowd gathers, weeping. Shecaniah speaks: “We have broken faith with our God… But even now there is hope for Israel in spite of this.” This is the grace of repentance. They propose a covenant to put away the foreign wives and children. It is a painful and controversial decision, and the chapter ends with a long list of names of those who did so. The text does not hide that this was costly and difficult.

We should read this with care. Some readers see in it a harsh ethnic rule. But the text emphasizes the matter of faith: the wives came from idolatrous peoples, and the people of God were in danger of losing their identity as the people who worship the LORD alone. For Christians, the principle is found in 2 Corinthians 6:14-18 and 1 Corinthians 7:12-16, where those already married to unbelievers are told to remain. The heart of the passage is not the specific remedy but the seriousness of repentance and the priority of covenant faithfulness to God.
connection: Daniel 9:4-19 shows the same kind of identifying prayer. 1 John 1:9: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us.” 2 Corinthians 7:10 says godly grief produces repentance that leads to salvation. Ruth, a Moabite, became part of the family of the Messiah by faith (Ruth 4:13-22; Matthew 1:5). Galatians 3:28 says that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek. Revelation 7:9 pictures every nation, tribe, people, and language worshiping together.
application:
Pray Ezra’s kind of prayer with “we” for your church or community. Confess sins that you share in, even when you were not directly involved.

Ask where your closest alliances and loyalties might draw you away from the LORD.

Receive Shecaniah’s words as encouragement: “Even now there is hope.”
prayerPrompts: Confess in your own words where you are ashamed before God.
Thank him for being righteous and merciful.
Ask him to help you turn from what you must leave.
